title: How would you estimate how many dentists the UK needs?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many dentists does the UK need?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: The UK needs roughly 45,000 full-time dentists: about 64M hours of dental work a year, divided by about 1,400 clinical hours one dentist can give. A check-ups-only shortcut gives about 36,000, and the gap between the two is the real lesson, because treatment, not check-ups, takes most of a dentist's time. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many dentists does the UK need?

"Need" can mean three things, so pick one out loud:

  • Demand: enough dentists to treat everyone who currently seeks care.
  • Clinical need: enough to treat everyone who should be seen, including people who never book.
  • Funded posts: what the NHS and private practices can pay for.
"I'll estimate full-time-equivalent dentists needed to meet today's demand: regular patients plus emergencies. I'll treat hygienists and therapists separately at the end."

The approach: hours of work ÷ hours per dentist

This is a capacity question: demand for dental time ÷ capacity of one dentist. The common shortcut counts check-ups only:

  • 68M people × 70% who see a dentist × 2 visits a year = 95.2M visits.
  • ÷ 2,640 visits per dentist (12 a day × 220 days) = about 36,000 dentists.

It misses fillings, crowns, root canals, extractions and emergencies, which take far longer than a check-up. Counting hours instead of visits fixes that, because a 20-minute check-up and a 90-minute root canal can sit in the same sum. It is the same idea as utilisation in an operations case.

Step by step

1. Demand in hours

Start with 68M people, of whom 70% (47.6M) see a dentist regularly.

Type of workAssumptionHours a year
Check-ups47.6M patients × 1.5 a year × 20 minutes23.8M
Treatment40% of patients (19.0M) × 2 hours each38.1M
Emergencies from irregular attenders30% of people (20.4M) × 10% × 1 hour2.0M
Total63.9M

Why 1.5 check-ups, not 2? Recall intervals depend on each patient's risk, and many low-risk adults are seen once a year or less. Why 2 hours of treatment? A filling might take 30 to 45 minutes, a crown or root canal several hours across visits; for the 40% who need something, 2 hours is a reasonable average.

2. Capacity of one dentist

220 working days × 6.5 hours with patients (the rest goes on notes, set-up and admin) = 1,430 clinical hours. Round to 1,400.

3. The answer

63.9M ÷ 1,400 = about 45,700 full-time-equivalent dentists. Call it 45,000.

Notice that treatment is 60% of the hours (38.1M of 63.9M), while check-ups are under 40%. That is why the check-ups-only shortcut comes in about a fifth too low.

Sanity check from a second angle

People per dentist. 68M ÷ 45,700 is about one dentist per 1,500 people. A practice with four dentists would then serve about 6,000 people, which sounds plausible for a high-street surgery.

Against the register. The General Dental Council had 45,580 dentists on its UK register in January 2025 (GDC). Registered is not the same as full-time and practising: many dentists work part time, and some work in hospitals, teaching or outside clinical care. So the full-time equivalent available for routine care is lower than 45,580, which suggests the UK is not over-supplied against our estimate of need.

What it means for a client

If the client is a government health department, the answer leads straight to levers beyond training more dentists: hygienists and therapists can take on check-ups and cleaning, longer recall intervals for low-risk patients free up time, and the national average hides local shortages. A country can have enough dentists overall and still have towns where nobody can get an appointment.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I estimate about 45,000 full-time dentists, from about 64 million hours of work a year at 1,400 clinical hours each. Treatment is 60% of that time, so it's the input I'd most want to check. The register has about 45,600 dentists, but many are part time, so on a full-time basis we're probably slightly short, and the bigger issue is likely where dentists are rather than how many."

A weak answer counts check-ups only, lands on 36,000, and concludes the UK has a big surplus because the register is higher. Both steps are wrong.

Common mistakes

  • Counting visits instead of time. Visits differ in length by a factor of ten. Use hours.
  • Assuming a dentist treats patients eight hours a day. Admin and set-up take a real share of the day.
  • Comparing to the headcount on a register. Compare full-time equivalents with full-time equivalents.
  • Forgetting the wider team. Hygienists and therapists do much of the preventive work in many practices.

Practise it

1. Hygienists take over half of all check-up time. How many dentists are needed now?

Show the answer

Check-up hours fall by half of 23.8M, which is 11.9M. New total: 63.9M − 11.9M = 52.0M hours. ÷ 1,400 = about 37,000 dentists. Shifting routine work to other professionals is one of the strongest levers a health system has.

2. The average dentist works four days a week, so 176 days a year. How many dentists (heads, not FTEs) are needed?

Show the answer

Capacity per dentist: 176 × 6.5 = 1,144 hours. 63.9M ÷ 1,144 = about 56,000 dentists. Part-time working raises the headcount needed by more than a fifth.

3. A campaign raises regular attendance from 70% to 80%. How many full-time dentists are needed?

Show the answer

Regular patients: 68M × 80% = 54.4M × 1.3 hours (check-ups plus average treatment) = 70.7M hours. Emergencies: 20% × 68M × 10% × 1 hour = 1.4M. Total 72.1M ÷ 1,400 = about 51,500 dentists, roughly 6,000 more. Success in prevention creates more demand first.

Where to practise next

The same capacity logic appears in piano tuners in Chicago and wedding photographers in the UK. For health system cases, read how hospitals and health systems work, and practise capacity questions in the market sizing drills.
